title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 7: A School Par Excellence for Judges
keywords: A School Par Excellence for Judges
scholarships for poor but deserving applicants
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's account of the long and tortuous journey to build the PhilJA Center in Tagaytay, which he calls a chronicle of faith, from the 1995 turnover of the property to the P300 million Japanese grant handed over during his own term.

His vision of transforming the Center, the first and only training school for the Philippine judiciary, into a national and ASEAN regional hub for continuing legal and judicial education, pre-judicature training, judicial career enhancement and specialized programs.

A proposed special school for young lawyers aspiring to be career judges, modeled on the Foreign Service Institute, with competitive entrance examinations and scholarships so that poverty bars no qualified entrant.

The link back to his program as Chief Justice: judicial education as the foundation-level attack on the 'I' for incompetence among the four ACID problems, in service of a judiciary marked by the four Ins.
sub_topics: The Center's origins: President Fidel V. Ramos turning over the 3.3-hectare facility to the Supreme Court on July 19, 1995 through the transfer of 51 percent of a sequestered corporation's shares at no cost, on the initiative of then Presidential Legal Counsel Antonio T. Carpio.

The cornerstone laid on November 23, 1998 under Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa, and the design and structural adjustments needed to convert a former recreation club into a training institution with more lecture rooms, offices and dining lounges.

CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.'s search for external funding after government funds failed to come: the June 2000 application under Japan's Grant Assistance Program, its suspension in 2004, and the new request through the Non-Project Grant Assistance Counter Value Fund.
Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki's handover of the P300 million NPGA grant on January 26, 2006, during CJP's term as Chief Justice.

Preparations already under way: the Project Implementation Committee created at the February 22, 2006 Action Planning Workshop, the approved Terms of Reference, budget and timelines for the Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design and Project Management Consultancy, referral to the APJR Bids and Awards Committee, and 12 expressions of intent to bid, with construction expected to commence the next year.
International linkages: the cooperation agreement he signed with Spain on June 30, 2006 for the Court, PhilJA and the JBC, and similar agreements being drawn up with France and the United Kingdom.

Regional discussions with Australia, Thailand, Indonesia and other Asia-Pacific countries on common curricula for justices and judges, arising from the Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network round-table and the Asian Justices Workshop on the Environment, both in March 2006.

Philippine leadership in regional judicial education through the Asia-Pacific Judicial Education Forum, with PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera as Executive Committee chairperson and IOJT deputy regional president for Asia and the Pacific.

The renewed focus on judicial science and court technology: Atty. Emmanuel L. Caparas named chairperson of PhilJA's Court Technology Department with Attys. Jesus M. Disini Jr. and Ray C. Espinosa as members, helping link the Case Flow Management Committee with the Court Management Information System.

The proposed career-judge school: competitive examinations and interviews to gauge preparedness and suitability, scholarships and financial assistance for poor but deserving applicants, and judges deep in ethical and moral formation as well as steeped in the law.
Foreign models under study for the school's organization, structure and licentiates or diplomates: Japan, Korea, Australia and France.

His December 21, 2005 vow restated -- four Ins, moral courage against influence, interference, indifference and insolence, and imperviousness to the plague of 'ships' -- and his commitment to continue the APJR.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' recounted what Chief Justice Panganiban called a chronicle of faith: the long and tortuous journey to build the Philippine Judicial Academy's Center in Tagaytay. He traced it from July 19, 1995, when President Fidel V. Ramos turned over the 3.3-hectare property to the Supreme Court through the free transfer of 51 percent of a sequestered corporation's shares on the initiative of then Presidential Legal Counsel Antonio T. Carpio, through the cornerstone laid on November 23, 1998 under Chief Justice Narvasa, to the funding detour in which Chief Justice Davide's June 2000 application under Japan's Grant Assistance Program was overtaken by that program's suspension in 2004 and had to be recoursed through the Non-Project Grant Assistance Counter Value Fund. The P300 million grant was finally handed over by Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki on January 26, 2006, during his own term. He reported the preparations already made -- a Project Implementation Committee from the February 22, 2006 Action Planning Workshop, approved terms of reference, budget and timelines for the architectural design, referral to the APJR Bids and Awards Committee, and 12 prospective bidders -- with construction expected to begin the following year. He then set out the ambition: to raise the first and only training school for the Philippine judiciary into a national and ASEAN regional hub for continuing legal education, pre-judicature training, career enhancement and specialized programs, supported by cooperation agreements with Spain and, in prospect, France and the United Kingdom, and by regional moves toward a common judicial curriculum. He proposed as well a special school for aspiring career judges modeled on the Foreign Service Institute, entered by competitive examination but open to poor applicants through scholarships. He closed by tying the project to his ACID agenda, arguing the campaign against corrosive judicial incompetence could be waged faster if begun at the foundations of judicial training.
